module.title: Normal Anatomy vs Pathology
module.goal: Train learners to differentiate normal anatomical structures and radiographic artifacts from pathology through pattern recognition and visual discrimination.

objectives.text: Correctly classify radiographic findings as normal anatomy, radiographic artifact, or pathology.
Identify common normal anatomical structures on radiographs (mental foramen, maxillary sinus, nutrient canals).
Differentiate radiographic artifacts and normal variations from caries or periapical pathology.
Correctly identify false-positive trap cases (cervical burnout, overlapping contacts, mental foramen).
Use radiographic features (shape, border definition, location, symmetry) to justify a finding as normal or pathologic.
Avoid overdiagnosing normal anatomical structures or artifacts as pathology.
Demonstrate improved accuracy in distinguishing normal anatomy from pathology after AI dialogue or annotation review.

cases.name: Mental Foramen
cases.finding: A well-defined, round radiolucency is projected over the apex of the mandibular left second premolar. The patient is asymptomatic and the tooth tests vital.

feedback.Normal anatomy: Correct. This is the mental foramen — a normal opening in the mandible where the mental nerve exits. Its round shape, corticated border, and location near the premolar apices give it away.
feedback.Radiographic artifact: Close, but this is a true anatomical structure, not an artifact. The mental foramen is a normal opening in the mandible — reclassify it as normal anatomy.
feedback.Pathology: This is the classic false-positive. A round, corticated radiolucency at the premolar apex with a vital tooth is the mental foramen, not a periapical lesion — calling it pathology is an overdiagnosis.

identify.feedback_correct: Right — the mental foramen sits in the mandibular premolar region and can superimpose on a premolar apex.
identify.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The location (mandibular premolar apex) and round, corticated appearance point to the mental foramen.

justify.prompt: Which feature best supports a NORMAL interpretation?
options: Round shape with a corticated (well-defined) border at the premolar apex, and an intact lamina dura on a vital tooth
Ill-defined borders with external root resorption
Loss of lamina dura and a widened periodontal ligament space
The finding is associated with a non-vital, symptomatic tooth
justify.correct: Round shape with a corticated (well-defined) border at the premolar apex, and an intact lamina dura on a vital tooth
justify.explain: A corticated border plus an intact lamina dura on a vital tooth argues strongly against a periapical lesion, which would show loss of lamina dura and an ill-defined radiolucency.

cases.trap: Frequently mistaken for periapical pathology at a premolar apex.
cases.review_hint: Check the tooth's vitality and trace the lamina dura. A corticated foramen border with intact lamina dura on a vital tooth means normal anatomy — not a lesion.
features: At or near the premolar apices

cases.name: Cervical Burnout
cases.finding: A wedge-shaped radiolucency appears at the cervical region of a molar — between the enamel cap and the alveolar crest — on both the mesial and distal surfaces.

feedback.Radiographic artifact: Correct. This is cervical burnout — an optical artifact from the sharp drop in X-ray absorption between the enamel and the alveolar bone. It is not a real lesion.
feedback.Normal anatomy: Not an anatomical structure — it's an imaging artifact (cervical burnout) produced by differential absorption at the cervical region.
feedback.Pathology: This is the common overdiagnosis: cervical burnout is mistaken for root/cervical caries. The symmetric, ill-defined cervical radiolucency with no cavitation is an artifact, not decay.

identify.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
identify.feedback_correct: Yes — the symmetric cervical radiolucency between enamel and crest is classic cervical burnout.
identify.feedback_incorrect: Reconsider. Caries and abrasion tend to be discrete and often cavitated; burnout is a symmetric, fading optical effect at the cervical region.

justify.prompt: Which feature best supports an ARTIFACT (not caries)?
options: Symmetric, ill-defined radiolucency confined between the enamel edge and crestal bone, fading gradually, with no cavitation
A discrete, well-cavitated radiolucency undermining the enamel
Radiolucency extending into the pulp chamber
Asymmetric lesion on a single proximal surface with sclerotic margins
justify.correct: Symmetric, ill-defined radiolucency confined between the enamel edge and crestal bone, fading gradually, with no cavitation
justify.explain: Burnout is symmetric on both proximal surfaces and fades gradually because it is an absorption effect; caries is usually a discrete, often cavitated lesion.

cases.trap: Commonly mistaken for cervical or root-surface caries.
cases.review_hint: Look for symmetry and cavitation. Burnout is symmetric on both proximal surfaces and fades gradually; caries is a discrete, often cavitated lesion.

cases.name: Nutrient Canal Mimic
cases.finding: A thin, vertical linear radiolucency runs through the alveolar bone between the mandibular central incisors.

feedback.Normal anatomy: Correct. This is a nutrient canal — a normal vascular channel in the alveolar bone. Its uniform width and thin corticated walls are the giveaway.
feedback.Radiographic artifact: It's a real anatomical channel, not an artifact. A uniform, corticated linear radiolucency in bone is a nutrient canal — normal anatomy.
feedback.Pathology: Overdiagnosis trap. A uniform-width, corticated linear radiolucency in bone is a nutrient canal, not a vertical root fracture or lesion.

identify.feedback_correct: Correct — nutrient canals are common between the mandibular incisors, especially in thin bone.
identify.feedback_incorrect: Reconsider. A fracture crosses the tooth/root and lacks cortication; this uniform, corticated channel lies in bone.

justify.prompt: Which feature best supports a NORMAL interpretation?
options: Uniform-width radiolucency with thin corticated (tram-track) walls, running within bone rather than through a root
A jagged line crossing the root with displacement of fragments
A widening radiolucency destroying the surrounding trabecular bone
An expansile, corticated cyst displacing adjacent roots
justify.correct: Uniform-width radiolucency with thin corticated (tram-track) walls, running within bone rather than through a root
justify.explain: Nutrient canals are uniform in width with corticated walls and lie in bone; fractures cross the root, are irregular, and lack cortication.

cases.trap: Mistaken for a vertical root fracture or a bony lesion.
cases.review_hint: Uniform width + corticated tram-track walls + located in bone = nutrient canal. Fractures cross the root, are irregular, and lack cortication.
features: Runs within bone, not through a root

cases.name: Maxillary Sinus Superimposition
cases.finding: A large radiolucent area with a thin, continuous white superior border overlies the roots of the maxillary molars. The roots appear to project into it.

feedback.Normal anatomy: Correct. The radiolucency is the maxillary sinus superimposed over the molar roots. The thin, intact corticated floor confirms it is air-filled sinus, not a lesion.
feedback.Radiographic artifact: It's a real anatomical space (the maxillary sinus), not an artifact — reclassify as normal anatomy.
feedback.Pathology: Overdiagnosis trap. The radiolucency is the maxillary sinus; the intact corticated floor means there is no periapical destruction — not pathology.

identify.feedback_correct: Correct — the maxillary sinus routinely superimposes over posterior maxillary roots.
identify.feedback_incorrect: Reconsider. The location above the posterior maxillary roots and a thin corticated floor point to the maxillary sinus.

justify.prompt: Which feature best supports a NORMAL interpretation?
options: A large radiolucency bounded by a thin, intact corticated floor, with roots projecting into it and no bone destruction
Loss of the lamina dura around the molar apices with an ill-defined radiolucency
An expansile radiolucency destroying the sinus floor
A well-corticated cyst centered on a single non-vital root apex
justify.correct: A large radiolucency bounded by a thin, intact corticated floor, with roots projecting into it and no bone destruction
justify.explain: An intact, continuous corticated sinus floor means the radiolucency is air within the sinus; a periapical lesion would erode the lamina dura and floor.

cases.trap: Sinus floor mistaken for periapical pathology near the molar roots.
cases.review_hint: Trace the thin corticated sinus floor. If it is intact and continuous, the radiolucency is air in the sinus — not a periapical lesion.
features: Large radiolucency over posterior maxillary roots
